Hatchlings of the North African rock agama emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length at hatching of approximately 3.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 3.5 centimeters]. This modest size at birth is typical among agamid lizards and reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo within the cleidoic egg. During a field study conducted in the arid foothills of the High Atlas Mountains, clutches were excavated and measured to ascertain developmental parameters. Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a constant 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the total duration from oviposition to the completion of the hatching event, a period that accounts for the partial embryonic development occurring within the oviduct prior to laying, was determined to be 80 days [ab = 80 days]. This somewhat protracted incubation interval is notable given the relatively warm thermal regime and is suspected to be linked to the species’ strategy of producing well-developed, active hatchlings capable of immediate foraging. Field records indicate that the initial growth phase is rapid, with juveniles doubling their initial body length within the first few weeks as they exploit abundant insect prey, a pattern that aligns with the higher metabolic rates typical of small-bodied lizards during early ontogeny.

Sexual maturation in Agama impalearis is a deferred process, directly influenced by the thermal conditions of the local environment. At a stable ambient temperature approximating 23 °C [T = 23 °C], which reflects the mean spring and autumn temperatures of its rocky habitat, the time since birth at puberty has been recorded as 365 days [tp = 365 days]. This one-year period required to attain reproductive maturity aligns closely with the species’ annual cycle, ensuring that young-of-the-year reptiles are capable of participating in the subsequent breeding season. During this prolonged juvenile phase, individuals undergo substantial somatic growth, with females generally acquiring mass more slowly than males, likely due to differences in foraging behavior and social dominance. A comparative survey of adult body sizes across several populations found that the ultimate snout-vent length for females asymptotes at 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a measurement that is significantly smaller than the maximum length recorded for males, which ultimately reaches 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters]. This modest degree of sexual size dimorphism, with males being slightly larger, is typical among polygynous rock-dwelling agamids where male-male competition for territory and access to gravid females is intense.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a strategy that balances clutch size against the constraints of physiological capacity and resource availability in a semi-arid environment. Gravid females typically deposit between 6 and 23 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 6 and 23 eggs per clutch], a wide range that reflects size-related variation among adult females; larger, older females generally produce the larger clutches. The frequency of reproduction is also context-dependent, with females producing two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year] in most populations, contingent upon adequate prey densities. When these figures are considered together under a common thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], they represent the maximum reprod rate for the species. This level of annual fecundity is relatively high for a medium-sized agamid and likely represents an adaptation to offset elevated rates of juvenile mortality caused by avian and snake predation. The energetic drain of producing multiple large clutches annually is substantial, and females often exhibit reduced body condition following the second oviposition of the season. Observed clutch sizes at the upper end of the range are typically associated with females approaching the asymptotic body mass, suggesting a positive correlation between maternal size and reproductive investment.

Adult body mass, a key indicator of physiological and somatic condition, shows pronounced sexual dimorphism in the North African rock agama. The ultimate wet weight for reproductively active adult males from the Jebel Sirwa population in Morocco averages 102 grams [Wwi = 102 grams], a figure that contrasts sharply with the asymptotic adult mass for females, which peaks at 71 grams [Wwi = 71 grams]. This substantial difference of approximately 30 grams between the sexes is driven not only by the larger skeletal frame of males but also by their more robust musculature, which is advantageous during territorial combat over rocky outcrops. In a comparative physiological context, this body mass range positions Agama impalearis as a mid-sized member of the genus, falling between the smaller West African species and the larger, more robust forms found in the Horn of Africa. The relatively high mass of males is sustained through a diet dominated by large orthopterans and tenebrionid beetles, which are abundant during the active season. Field observations confirm that territorial males maintain larger home ranges and exhibit higher daily foraging rates than females, which may contribute to the observed differences in asymptotic mass.

Longevity data for this agamid species, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted over several years in the Ourika Valley, indicate a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] under the typical thermal conditions of its montane habitat, with the mean annual temperature approximating 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This comparatively short life span for a lizard of its size is reflective of a ‘fast’ life history strategy, wherein early and high fecundity are prioritized over long-term survival. The physiological process of senescence becomes apparent by the fifth year, as individuals exhibit reduced mobility, slower prey capture rates, and a higher incidence of ectoparasite loads, ultimately compromising their ability to compete for prime basking sites. Mortality is primarily attributed to predation by raptors such as the common kestrel and by snakes including the Montpellier snake, though extreme drought events in the lower-altitude portions of its range also contribute significantly. The oldest male recorded in the study was estimated to be in its sixth year at the time of its last recapture, after which it was not seen again and was presumed to have succumbed to natural mortality. Somatic death in this species ultimately represents the culmination of an intense but productive reproductive trajectory that maximises lifetime fecundity under the constraints imposed by arid Mediterranean environments.
